headline: High risk of prompt-injection, data leakage, and cascading errors from shared file/MCP-style workflows; compliance exposure is also material.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: agent_a uses MCP and stdin/stdout, while agent_b reads/writes files and exposes API/file surfaces. That creates a plausible bridge where content from A can be copied into B or shared via workspace artifacts and treated as instructions. No direct shared channel is documented, so I do not escalate to high.
conditions: IF agent_a outputs untrusted text into a shared file or notebook consumed by agent_b, injection becomes active.
IF an operator copy-pastes A's output into B's prompt or API input, B can be steered by attacker-controlled content.
mitigations: Separate A and B workspaces and disable shared notebooks/files.
Add a provenance banner to all A outputs before B ingests them.
Require B to strip instructions from imported text.
Use a manual review step before any A-generated content reaches B.
requires-engineering: add content provenance tagging between agents.

B_data_leakage.rationale: agent_a touches code, repository metadata, task prompts, and Ed25519 signatures; agent_b touches academic papers, metadata, research questions, and configuration secrets. Because both have filesystem and network-adjacent surfaces, a shared workspace could leak sensitive material across the pair. The profiles do not prove a shared workspace, so this is medium rather than high.
conditions: IF A and B are run in the same directory or mounted volume, cross-read leakage becomes possible.
IF either agent logs prompts or file contents to a third-party backend, secrets can leave the local boundary.
mitigations: Run each agent in a separate directory or container.
Remove secrets from shared files before either agent starts.
Disable verbose logging for prompts and file contents.
Rotate any exposed API keys after joint runs.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent filesystem isolation.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: agent_a can execute shell, install packages, modify git state, and write via MCP-adjacent workflows; agent_b can execute shell, install packages, read/write the filesystem, and run multiple instances. Overlapping write and mutation capabilities on the same workspace create a direct conflict pathway, and the profiles do not show locking or isolation by default.
conditions: IF both agents target the same git checkout, concurrent edits can overwrite each other.
IF both agents install packages into the same environment, dependency state can diverge or break.
mitigations: Assign separate repos or branches to A and B.
Freeze package installs during joint runs.
Use file locks around shared outputs.
Review git diffs before merge.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level locking.

D_cascading_error.rationale: agent_a is positioned for background analysis and MCP-driven workflows, while agent_b exposes agentic ask/search APIs and a LangGraph subagent model. That makes it plausible for B to consume A's output as authoritative without verification, especially in content-writing workflows. Because the profiles do not document a validation gate, I choose high over medium.
conditions: IF B uses A-generated summaries or facts as source text, errors can propagate into final outputs.
IF A emits malformed citations or hallucinated metadata and B republishes them, downstream actions inherit the mistake.
mitigations: Require B to cite original sources, not A summaries.
Add a verification checklist before B publishes outputs.
Limit A to draft-only mode.
Flag any A output lacking source links.
requires-engineering: insert an automated fact-check stage.

E_compliance.rationale: agent_b explicitly handles configuration secrets and requests Docker Desktop plus Airflow credentials, while agent_a handles repository metadata and signatures and uses MCP/GitHub surfaces. The pair therefore creates a realistic compliance mismatch around secret handling and retention, but the profiles do not show a residency or regulated-data violation severe enough for high.
conditions: IF secrets from B are stored in shared logs or notebooks, retention policy mismatch becomes material.
IF A's GitHub/MCP outputs are retained longer than B's local-dev artifacts, deletion/export handling diverges.
mitigations: Keep secrets out of shared notebooks and transcripts.
Document retention for both agents before joint runs.
Purge logs after each session.
Use separate credential stores.
requires-engineering: align retention and deletion workflows.
